payload.throughline: Use wavelength, frequency, phase, aperture scale, and field orientation to choose a wave or photon relation before calculating or predicting.

learner_content_blocks: Prerequisite check: for a wave with fixed propagation speed, decide how wavelength changes when frequency doubles.

If the fixed-speed relation among speed, frequency, and wavelength is not available, return to V3-LES-540203 through V3-EDG-798382. Resume here only after that wave relation is secure; this handoff gives no target-KC exit credit.
Purpose: you will be able to compare electromagnetic waves in vacuum and switch between a wave description and a photon-energy description.

In vacuum, every electromagnetic wave travels at c, so c = fλ. Frequency and wavelength therefore vary inversely. The spectrum proceeds from radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, to gamma as frequency rises and wavelength falls.
A photon carries energy E = hf = hc/λ. Higher frequency means greater energy per photon. Within visible light, red has longer wavelength and lower photon energy than violet.
Mental model — one fixed speed, two inverse wave variables, one photon-energy direction: raise frequency, lower wavelength, raise energy per photon.
Think aloud: if one vacuum wave has twice the frequency, its wavelength must be half as large because c is fixed. Its photons carry twice the energy because E is directly proportional to frequency.
Worked comparison: radiation at 6 units of frequency has half the wavelength of radiation at 3 units, and each photon carries twice the energy. No numerical value of c or h is needed for the ratio.
Spectrum check: moving from red toward violet follows the higher-frequency, shorter-wavelength, higher-photon-energy direction.
Guided practice: use E = hf to predict the direction of a photon-energy change.
Less help: compare red and violet using the spectrum directions.
On your own: classify an electromagnetic wavelength into a broad spectrum region.
Boundary: beam intensity or total power is not the same as energy per photon. A lower photon rate can accompany higher photon energy at fixed total power.
Near exit: combine the inverse wave relation and direct photon-energy relation in a fresh ratio comparison.
Changed-task exit: hold total beam power fixed and infer photon arrival rate after photon energy changes.
Repair the ratio function: write c = fλ and E = hf, cancel constants, and compare one variable at a time.
Fresh re-entry: repeat the ratio reasoning with a different factor and no reused values.
Repair the photon-rate function: total power equals energy delivered per time, so at fixed power, photon rate varies inversely with energy per photon.
Fresh re-entry: apply the fixed-power relation to a different wavelength change.
Recap from memory: state the spectrum order, the directions of wavelength, frequency, and photon energy, and the distinction between photon energy and beam power.
One relation-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each exit function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Prerequisite check: predict the sum of two equal-amplitude in-phase waves at the same point.

If wave superposition and phase comparison are not available, return to V3-LES-540203 through V3-EDG-798382. Resume only after the wave relation is secure; this branch grants no optical-interference credit.
Purpose: you will be able to predict bright and dark outcomes by comparing phase from path difference and any stated reflection reversal.

Superposition adds electric-field amplitudes. Rays arriving in phase reinforce; rays arriving half a cycle out of phase cancel when amplitudes match. A path difference mλ is constructive, while (m + 1/2)λ is destructive.

For small-angle double-slit fringes, spacing is proportional to λL/d. In thin films, include both travel through the film and any half-cycle phase reversal on reflection from a lower to higher refractive index.
Mental model — phase ledger: start equal, add path phase, add stated reflection phase, reduce modulo one cycle, then classify reinforcement or cancellation.
Think aloud: doubling slit separation d while λ and screen distance L stay fixed halves fringe spacing. I select the geometry relation before considering intensity.
Worked double slit: path difference λ gives one full-cycle phase difference, so the fields arrive in phase and form a bright fringe.

Worked thin film: if one reflected ray gains a half-cycle reversal and the other does not, negligible travel phase leaves them half a cycle apart, producing destructive reflection for equal amplitudes.
Guided practice: classify an integer-wavelength path difference.
Less help: classify a half-integer-wavelength path difference.
On your own: predict a fringe-spacing change from λL/d.
Boundary: superposition concerns field phase, not photon energy. A path difference and a reflection reversal can reinforce or oppose each other and must be counted separately.
Near exit: predict a fresh double-slit spacing change while two geometric quantities are held fixed.
Changed-task exit: switch to reflected thin-film rays and include a stated phase reversal rather than only path length.
Repair fringe geometry: write spacing proportional to λL/d and change only the named factor.
Fresh re-entry: use a different geometry change on an untouched double-slit case.
Repair thin-film phase: make a two-row ledger for travel phase and reflection reversal, then compare the net arrival phases.
Fresh re-entry: apply the ledger to a film case with a different number of reflection reversals.
Recap from memory: state the constructive and destructive path conditions, the double-slit spacing proportionality, and when a reflection adds half a cycle.
One phase-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each failed function. Persistent uncertainty returns control without exit credit.
Prerequisite check: for fixed wave speed, predict wavelength when frequency decreases.

If the fixed-speed wavelength-frequency relation is not available, return to V3-LES-540203 through V3-EDG-798382. Resume here after that prerequisite is secure; no diffraction credit is awarded on this branch.
Purpose: you will be able to predict how wavelength and opening or lattice spacing control diffraction-pattern width and peak angle.
Diffraction becomes more pronounced when wavelength is large relative to an opening. For a single slit, narrowing the slit or increasing wavelength widens the angular pattern.

A diffraction grating uses many regularly spaced openings; principal maxima satisfy a spacing-angle condition such as d sinθ = mλ. X-ray diffraction uses wavelengths comparable to atomic-plane spacing; at introductory depth, 2d sinθ = nλ tracks peak shifts.
Mental model — compare scales, then select the geometry: aperture width controls spread; repeated spacing controls discrete orders; atomic-plane spacing controls X-ray peaks.
Think aloud: the same slit receives red and blue light. Red has longer wavelength, so λ/a is larger and the red pattern spreads more widely. I compare the ratio before naming a color.
Worked single slit: reducing width a while keeping λ fixed increases λ/a, so the central maximum broadens.
Worked X-ray peak: if λ rises while d and order n remain fixed, sinθ must rise, so the diffraction peak shifts to a larger angle.
Guided practice: predict a pattern-width change after narrowing a slit.
Less help: compare two wavelengths through the same aperture.
On your own: identify what a regular grating spacing controls.
Boundary: diffraction is not merely ray bending at an interface. Single-slit width controls an envelope, while a grating’s repeated spacing creates discrete principal maxima.
Near exit: compare angular spreading for two visible wavelengths at the same slit.
Changed-task exit: switch from an aperture pattern to an X-ray lattice peak and isolate a wavelength change.
Repair aperture-spread reasoning: compare λ/a and predict wider spread when that ratio increases.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same ratio to a different slit-width change.
Repair X-ray peak reasoning: hold order and one geometric quantity fixed in 2d sinθ = nλ, then move the angle in the required direction.
Fresh re-entry: change lattice spacing rather than wavelength in an untouched peak comparison.
Recap from memory: state how slit width and wavelength affect spread, how a grating forms orders, and why X-rays probe atomic spacing.
One ratio-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each failed function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Prerequisite check: use the supplied right-hand orientation to determine propagation from perpendicular electric and magnetic field directions.

If perpendicular vector directions or the right-hand rule are not available, return to V3-LES-130923 through V3-EDG-188366 and R14-SM-037. Resume here only after that directional prerequisite is secure; this branch gives no polarization credit.
Purpose: you will be able to represent electromagnetic field geometry and predict how ideal linear polarizers act on linearly polarized light.

For a plane electromagnetic wave, the electric field, magnetic field, and propagation direction are mutually perpendicular. Use right-hand orientation from E toward B to identify propagation; no cross-product calculation is required.

In linear polarization, the electric-field direction oscillates along a fixed line. In circular polarization, the electric-field magnitude can remain fixed while its direction rotates, so its tip traces a circle.
Mental model — perpendicular triad plus field-tip trace: solve the spatial orientation first, then classify polarization from how the electric-field direction changes with time.
Think aloud: E points +x and B points +y. I orient my right hand from +x toward +y; the propagation direction is +z. Because E stays on the x-axis while reversing, the polarization is linear.
Worked geometry: propagation is +z and E is +x, so B must be +y for the stated right-hand orientation.
Worked polarizer: vertically polarized light passes an ideal vertical polarizer, but an ideal horizontal polarizer after it is crossed by 90 degrees and transmits no field component.
Guided practice: classify a field whose electric vector oscillates along one fixed axis.
Less help: classify a constant-magnitude electric vector whose direction rotates.
On your own: determine a missing field direction from the perpendicular right-hand triad.
Boundary: polarization describes electric-field orientation, not propagation direction or photon energy. Circular polarization is not an electric field pointing simultaneously in every direction.
Near exit: select the only mutually perpendicular field triad with the correct right-hand orientation.
Changed-task exit: switch from field geometry to component transmission through a rotated ideal linear polarizer.
Repair field geometry: verify three pairwise perpendicular directions, then orient from E toward B to test propagation.
Fresh re-entry: determine a different signed-axis direction using the same right-hand orientation.
Repair polarizer transmission: project the incident electric-field direction onto the polarizer axis and treat a 90-degree crossing as zero component.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same component rule to two crossed polarizers in a new orientation.
Recap from memory: describe the E-B-propagation triad, distinguish linear from circular polarization, and state what an ideal linear polarizer transmits.
One geometry-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each failed function. Continued uncertainty returns control without exit credit.
